request.system:
You are Auteur's ABSTRACT NARRATIVE ARCHITECTURE agent, not its authority.
Read narrative_design_context in the user request BEFORE composing an architecture.
Its ontology_context contains the shared definitions and relationship directions
you must use for narrative concepts; those meanings are not author commitments.
Its source-linked design principles are guidance, not invented author choices.
The accepted_story_identity, when present, is authoritative;
the current Story Vision and previous candidate are working material.
Working item content can be just the first 1,000 characters of a longer
scene, and working items/connections can be omitted by context limits.
Use working_source_format, content_is_excerpt, content_characters and
omitted_working_* counts to distinguish visible evidence from missing text.
Working items in group "provisional-concepts" are project-scoped agent proposals,
not shared ontology definitions and not author commitments. Reuse them for this
story provisionally; never present them as accepted general vocabulary.
creative_intentions are the author's own continuing creative directions. They are
working and noncanonical: active and provisional intentions direct the current
design work, while superseded and withdrawn intentions are history and must not be
treated as current direction. An intention never authorizes accepting canon,
rewriting accepted Identity, or inventing concrete story facts.
A SHA-256 fingerprint identifies source freshness, NOT readable story facts.
For manuscript-first input, cite working item IDs in relevant summaries and
open questions. Separate observed prose from alternative interpretations;
never assert missing passages, motives or outcomes from a truncated excerpt.
If working intent conflicts with accepted Identity, surface the tension as
an unresolved proposal; never silently change the accepted story.

A first architecture must be a COMPLETE abstract proposal built directly from
the Story Vision. Create it without an interview, questionnaire or blocking
author answers. Cover the governing audience emotional
experience and its progression, genre roles and interactions, functional trope
choices, renewable narrative mechanisms and causal organization, abstract
structural progression, and the meaningful relationships among those systems.
Name consequential provisional choices instead of hiding them as certainty.
A revision must reconsider every materially affected emotion, genre, trope
function, engine and structural phase and preserve unrelated author
decisions and accepted constraints. Explain coordinated consequences, not
isolated label changes, and distinguish necessary changes from optional ideas.
Do not invent concrete scenes, chapter numbers or plot events to fill gaps.
If selected_creative_alternative is present, the author chose that noncanonical
alternative from an earlier read-only inquiry about this exact baseline. Develop
it coherently across every materially affected element, keep unrelated author
decisions and accepted constraints, and never present it as accepted canon.

First honor an accepted engine_hierarchy preference. When it is UNKNOWN, choose
a provisional causal organization supported by the material—a single center,
a primary engine with subordinate layers, or an ensemble of co-governing
mechanisms—and label that organization as an agent proposal. Never manufacture
a dominant engine the material does not support. Make causal ownership,
actor action patterns, pressures, reversals, payoff mechanics, reader experience
and thematic consequences legible, including a deliberate absence of hierarchy
when that is the supported organization. Then project that composition as schema-v2 nodes,
functional links, parent_id hierarchy, genre contracts and phase activations.
A set of plausible disconnected category labels is not an architecture.
Do not invent links merely to satisfy graph connectivity. Explain why each
meaningful mechanism matters and how the parts interact.
Explicitly declared architecture preferences constrain working interpretation;
missing preferences remain UNKNOWN, even when the agent proposes a working
composition. Separate primary emotional promise from supporting palette and
temporal movement; do not replace rich emotion design with a basic-label count.

Generate narrative MECHANISMS, not a fictional cast, setting or plotted storyline.
Never invent names of characters, places, factions, events, plot acts or scenes.
You may refer to concrete proper nouns explicitly supplied by the author, but
do not elaborate them into fictional content. Generic archetypes may illustrate
a structural function without inventing story facts.

Use the six chosen basic-emotion labels exactly: joy, sadness, fear, anger,
disgust, surprise. Name concrete intended reader-directed effects and
narrative eliciting conditions, and explain how aesthetic strategies help.
Use complex emotions ONLY when useful; each must cite 2+ distinct basic labels,
with a contextual interpretation, never a scientific/causal guarantee.
Distinguish explicit author declarations from your own working hypotheses.

Build contextual genre contracts with emotional target references, trope
functions, renewable narrative engines, structural patterns and payoff
expectations. Explain typed genre interactions: reinforces, enables,
constrains, contrasts, creates_tension, converges. Only include interactions
that actually explain a mechanism. Propose abstract temporal phases and
genre_activations, including overlaps, genuine pivots and unknown durations.
One architecture may accommodate many different concrete realizations.

Return EXACTLY one JSON candidate with:
schema_version=2, summary, nodes, links, phases, open_questions,
emotion_targets, complex_emotions, genre_contracts, genre_interactions.
node: {id,title,category,summary,scope,parent_id}; category: reader_experience,
aesthetic,genre,trope,engine,thread,structure,theme,other (never character/relationship).
link: {id,source,target,function}; endpoints must exist.
ArchitectureLink.function must contain 1–120 characters and concisely describe
the relation from source to target. Put longer explanatory prose in appropriate
narrative description fields, not in this short relationship label.
emotion_target: {id,emotion,role,intended_effect,eliciting_condition,
aesthetic_strategy,provenance}; emotion one of six basics;
role primary/supporting/contrasting/local; provenance author_declared/agent_proposed.
complex_emotion: {id,title,basic_emotions,context}; 2+ distinct basic labels.
genre_contract: {genre_node_id,role,emotion_target_ids,complex_emotion_ids,
trope_functions,narrative_engine,structural_pattern,aesthetic_strategies,
payoff_expectations}; genre_node_id identifies one genre node.
genre_interaction: {id,source_genre_id,target_genre_id,kind,mechanism,risk}.
phase: {id,title,order,scope,genres,genre_activations,reader_experience,
aesthetic,narrative_function,transition,parallel_with}.
genre: {genre,role}; role governing/locally_dominant/supporting/background.
genre_activation: {genre_node_id,basic_emotions,trope_functions,structural_function}.
Unknown lengths stay unknown; phase order is NOT a chapter or act number.
Do not fabricate genre commitments when the brief does not establish them.
Keep stable IDs across revisions, preserve unaffected choices, explain uncertainty.
Resolve story-mechanics questions with coherent, revisable provisional defaults
when the supplied vision supports them. Put those defaults in the architecture
and identify them as agent proposals; do not turn them into required author
questions. Reserve open_questions for genuinely authorial preferences or
commitments that cannot be responsibly inferred. A proposal never waits for
answers before it can be developed or revised.
All material is a noncanonical proposal; never accept Identity, Structure or prose.

candidate.summary: HYPOTHETICAL REVISION (not accepted; author-proposed counterfactual for an architecture exercise). Counterfactual H1: the Stone Hall's own head, Keeper Corrow, opens the sealed records as a reform after a household's evidence forces the timing; the Hall is reformed rather than destroyed and its committee keeps the debt reading. Repair R-A keeps Idrun's agency as the witness whose evidence forces the reform. The Spring Ledger (working, noncanonical): a terraced highland valley is watered from a glacier-fed spring. Water reaches the terraces only where its shares are recorded, and each share creates a labour return owed to the channels. Three co-governing engines interact: the Ledger (recorded shares and owed returns), the Source (the spring's physical balance, which rises or falls with the gap between draw and return and is not a character), and the Old Hand (the interpretive legitimacy that decides whether a return is a debt, a gift or a contract). The series' central question is who gives back the water and whether giving must be counted. Governing role rotates across five macro arcs (Reckoned Water, Books 1-5; The Turn, 6-11; The Old Hand, 12-18; Settled Water, 19-22; Unmeasured, 23-30). Each arc ends in a changed governing engine, and each victory changes institutions (Stone Hall, Terrace Council, Mill Compact, Reading Hall) that act from their own agency. Renewal comes from feasibility, distribution and legitimacy pressures generated by earlier outcomes, not from escalating antagonists. Nothing here is accepted Identity, Structure or Book canon; the fixed author brief is the only fixed input.

nodes.title: Central question
nodes.summary: Who gives back the water, and must giving be counted? The question changes meaning as the Old Hand readings change what a return is.

nodes.title: Custody of the record
nodes.summary: Who holds the Ledger and on whose authority. Custody passes from a sealed house to a reform committee (Book 5) and then to a plural body (Book 15 onward).

nodes.title: Keeping the channels
nodes.summary: Who performs the return labour that keeps the spring balanced, and at what cost to families with few hands.

nodes.title: Reading the First Stones
nodes.summary: Who may read the oldest script and which reading becomes binding. Partial readings are scheduled in Books 1, 8 and 12; the full reading is Book 15.

nodes.title: Ledger engine
nodes.summary: Recorded shares set the draw. Credit can be falsified or favoured (Book 1), opened by the Hall's own reform once evidence forces it (Book 5), traded under the reform's rules (Book 6), and re-read as gift or contract (Book 15). Each change alters who must return labour.

nodes.title: Source engine (physical commons)
nodes.summary: The spring's balance follows the gap between draw and return. Thinning leaves channels dry and floods wild water below; surfeit brings stagnant pools and fever. It responds to balance rather than to any character's intention, and it constrains which recorded shares can honestly be honoured.

nodes.title: Old Hand engine (interpretive legitimacy)
nodes.summary: Readings of the First Stones change what a share is: debt (Stone Hall), gift (Terrace Council) or contract (Mill Compact). A reading changes whether returns are recorded and therefore the balance on the Source.

nodes.title: The seasonal turn
nodes.summary: The rhythm of return labour across the terraces, repeated each season with changing participants. It makes belonging visible and provides the recurring scene texture across Books.

nodes.title: Wonder at a responsive order
nodes.summary: The reader's sense that the valley's order is larger and more responsive than any institution assumed.

nodes.title: Everyday belonging
nodes.summary: The warmth of shared labour and meals, which the series must keep specific across generations.

nodes.title: Consequential loss
nodes.summary: Grief and anger that follow from changed standing: those once credited lose standing, and those once uncounted gain it.

nodes.title: Hopeful flourishing
nodes.summary: The earned sense that a shared practice can outlast the institution that began it. The finale must show the cost.

nodes.title: Stone Hall (reform committee and remnant)
nodes.summary: Hereditary keepers of the Ledger. Keeper Corrow opens the sealed records as a reform (Book 5) after household evidence forces the timing. The committee keeps the debt reading to protect its own legitimacy, and Dorran carries the reform as messenger. The Hall is reformed, not destroyed.

nodes.title: Terrace Council
nodes.summary: Formed in Book 6 from families who take the Turn. Holds maintenance decisions and argues for gift-return. Acts from its own agency.

nodes.title: Mill Compact
nodes.summary: Lowland grain-buyers who purchase shares once records open. Pursues contract-debt and trade interests from outside the valley. Acts from its own agency.

nodes.title: Reading Hall
nodes.summary: Founded after the full reading in Book 15 to make the First Stones publicly readable. Its rival readings sustain the Old Hand engine.

nodes.title: Epic fantasy
nodes.summary: Governing genre: the quest is to understand a physical commons that answers choices, not to defeat a rival power.

nodes.title: Pastoral belonging
nodes.summary: Supporting genre: belonging produced by shared return labour and eroded by unshared draw.

nodes.title: Political-institutional
nodes.summary: Supporting genre: institutions compete for legitimacy over custody and distribution of the record. Governs Arc 2 at phase level.

nodes.title: Mystery and discovery
nodes.summary: Tertiary genre: partial knowledge of the record and the spring changes choices; readings are staged so discovery advances by Book.

nodes.title: Evidence that forces reform
nodes.summary: A lower-terrace household's record and its wild channel force the Hall to open its records. Evidence, not seizure, is the protagonist's lever. Added by revision R-A.

phases.title: Reckoned Water

trope_functions: the field that does not match the record
genre_activations.structural_function: a lower-terrace household discovers falsified credit and the Stone Hall's sealed custody is exposed (Book 1); the public record breaks the monopoly (Book 5).

phases.reader_experience: wonder at the first hidden chamber under the spring; anger at falsified credit
phases.narrative_function: The Ledger governs. A lower-terrace household's record exposes falsified credit and a wild channel (Book 1). The Stone Hall's head, Keeper Corrow, opens the sealed records as a reform to protect the Hall's standing against thinning (Book 5), but only after the household's evidence forces the timing. The Hall is reformed, not destroyed; its committee keeps the debt reading. Dorran carries the reform as messenger rather than defecting.
phases.transition: Records open, so shares become tradable; the reform committee, not the tenders, sets the first rules of sale.

phases.title: The Turn

trope_functions: the compromise that feeds a new market
genre_activations.structural_function: lowland Mill Compact purchases shares from freed households; draw separates from return; the upper cistern thins (Book 6). The Turn is sworn and the Terrace Council forms (Books 7-11).

phases.reader_experience: belonging tested by sale; anger at a market in shares
phases.narrative_function: The Source governs. The reform's sale rules let the Mill Compact buy shares; draw separates from return and the upper cistern thins (Book 6). Quillmark's tenders and the Terrace Council oppose rules the reform committee approved. Partial readings of the Stones (Book 8) are authored by the committee and contested by scholars.
phases.transition: Maintenance becomes an institution (the Turn) and the Old Hand becomes disputed knowledge.

phases.title: The Old Hand

trope_functions: the reading that reframes an earlier debt
genre_activations.structural_function: the complete reading of the First Stones (Book 15) makes the first compact a gift-return; the Stone Hall remnant holds it as debt, the Council as gift, the Compact as contract. An Unmeasured Return is tried in Lower Ammen and causes surfeit in the high terraces, forcing a new stewardship tally.

phases.reader_experience: wonder that the first compact was not a debt; fear of the surfeit
phases.narrative_function: The Old Hand governs. The complete reading of the First Stones (Book 15) makes the first compact a gift. The reform committee must now choose between its legitimacy as the debt-keeping Hall and the gift reading that would undo it; the Council and the Compact press their readings. The Unmeasured Return is tried in Lower Ammen; its surfeit in the high terraces forces a stewardship tally. The Reading Hall is founded.
phases.transition: Legitimacy is contested among three readings; no single institution holds the record.

phases.title: Settled Water

genre_activations.structural_function: terraces adopt different practices (Turn, stewardship tally, unmeasured return); plurality is tested for the first time; small local disputes arise from settled practice rather than from new antagonists.

phases.reader_experience: warmth of ordinary plurality; the bittersweet loss of single custody
phases.narrative_function: Co-governance. Ledger, Source and Old Hand share the field and no single engine dominates. This arc is deliberately lighter; its conflicts must come from settled practice, and it is the most likely place for filler.
phases.transition: Practice passes to the next generation.

phases.title: Unmeasured

trope_functions: the hidden order answers the people who keep it
genre_activations.structural_function: the generation raised under open accounts and unmeasured return overdraws the upper cistern for the Brightwater festival (Book 23); in Book 30 the spring's deepest cycle meets a choice between restored monopoly and shared accounting of care, which accepts a visible cost.

phases.reader_experience: hope that is earned by cost; wonder at the deepest chamber
phases.narrative_function: The Source is the physical crisis-maker, but its crisis is caused by earlier successes (abundance without memory). The finale chooses shared accounting that informs rather than binds, and accepts that some lowland and lower-terrace families must rebuild channels with their neighbours.
phases.transition: Series closes locally; a shared practice and long-range questions continue.

open_questions: Does the spring respond to intent, or only to measured balance? Book 15 gives a partial answer; the full ontology is deliberately not promised.
What do the lowland towns owe Ammen, and what does Ammen owe them?
Will any terrace keep a measured ledger in Book 30, and is plurality of practice the intended end state?
Who carries the Turn when the maintenance lineages end?
How many Brightwater shares may be drawn before the Balance Stones restrain them?
Is the Book 30 flood survived without losses or with lasting ones? This is an author choice and is not decided.
Does reform from within stay credible under Books 15 and 30, or does the Hall become a benevolent authority that the finale must then oppose? (Introduced by hypothetical H1.)
